children: By Tripti Lahiri

For more than a century, India's Tata business empire prided itself as a steward of a brand of capitalism that gives priority to social welfare and the country's national interests over short-term corporate strategy and the pursuit of personal wealth for its owners.

Now, pressure from authorities to list the main holding vehicle for the group's sprawling interests has set off an internal battle that threatens the future of one of India's most storied conglomerates.

The fight is between Noel Tata, the 69-year-old scion of the Tata founding family, and N. Chandrasekaran, chairman of Tata Sons, the main holding company that controls businesses spanning manufacturing, corporate services, steel, cars, salt and aviation.
On Sept. 17, four board members outvoted Tata to grant a third term to Chandrasekaran. Noel Tata has declared the vote illegal, a stance the board disputes.

Behind the clash is a 2022 decision by India's central bank to order the company to seek a stock market listing for Tata Sons, in compliance with new rules governing systemically important investment firms. Tata Sons is categorized as an investment firm because it holds stakes in Tata subsidiaries and can inject capital into them.

Days before the recent board meeting, India's central bank reiterated the order. Under Chandrasekaran's leadership, Tata Sons has said it would comply. However, Noel Tata, who heads the bloc of charities that owns two-thirds of Tata Sons, vehemently opposes a listing.

The group was "conceived as national service carried on through business...and the structure of its ownership is what has allowed it to remain so," Tata said at the board meeting. Tata Sons' "dividends fund hospitals, universities and research for which no shareholder will ever be repaid. Its capital has repeatedly been placed at risk for reasons no analyst would have endorsed and from which the country has nonetheless benefited."

The company, whose early trading days date to the 19th century and the era of British rule, once exported opium to China and sold cotton to Britain when the American Civil War dried up supplies. It has long positioned itself as a partner to India's nation-building efforts.

Tata patriarch Jamsetji Tata laid the foundations of large-scale steel manufacturing in colonial-era India. Later, the family also established the country's first airline and founded prominent centers of scientific and social research.

Members of the Tata family have been noticeably absent from global billionaire lists even as families of newer Indian conglomerates have climbed those rankings. That stems in part from a decision by the Tatas about a century ago to set up trusts that would hold controlling stakes in the Tata Group, thus capping their personal wealth.
Tata's 26 listed firms had a market capitalization of nearly $280 billion in March. In recent weeks, the leadership turmoil has dragged down the prices of some group firms.
The trusts receive hundreds of millions of dollars in dividends from Tata Sons. In the year ended March 2025, they spent more than $100 million on education, health and other social programs.

Harish Salve, a lawyer advising Tata Sons and Chandrasekaran, said the central bank's listing push was meant to "ensure that companies which have access to large public funds and huge assets which are important for the economy are controlled in a manner consistent with the highest norms of governance."
The Shapoorji Pallonji Group, which holds about 18% of Tata Sons and has been seeking to exit part of its stake, has welcomed the Reserve Bank of India's push.

The recent board meeting marked an about-face for Chandrasekaran's fortunes. Chandrasekaran, who has been chairman of Tata Sons since 2017, had said he would step down at the end of his current term next February, citing a lack of support from a board member he didn't name. Noel Tata was widely believed to have been that board member.
But at the recent meeting, all the board members apart from Tata voted to give him a third term. The board also said it would comply with the central bank's directives.
That included Venu Srinivasan, a scion of an automotive industry dynasty, who along with Noel Tata represents the Tata Trusts on the Tata Sons board, but nevertheless voted for Chandrasekaran.

Chandrasekaran had earlier hoped for a unanimous reappointment, but agreed to stay on despite the split vote. He chose to remain given the critical juncture the firm faces, amid massive new investments and a directive to go public that he is committed to meeting, said a person familiar with his thinking.
Noel Tata didn't respond to requests for comment.

Some corporate governance experts attribute the rebellion Noel Tata is facing to a staggered succession by his half-brother Ratan Tata, who died in 2024. Ratan Tata relinquished his role as chairman of Tata Sons years earlier, but retained his position as head of the trusts until his death.

Noel Tata has since found himself jockeying for influence with other trustees as well as Chandrasekaran, Tata observers say. If Noel Tata had been allowed to take over at the Tata Trusts earlier and found his footing while Ratan Tata was still alive, the company would face less disruption now, said Shriram Subramanian, managing director of InGovern Research Services, a Bangalore-based proxy advisory firm.

Proponents of listing the firm say that the move would provide more transparency on how the company is spending its funds and would allow Tata Sons to raise capital directly for its heavy investments in semiconductors and electronics manufacturing, efforts India's government is eager to see prosper.
Tata is Apple's only homegrown assembler of iPhones in India. The company also faces heavy expenses from its efforts to turn around loss-making flagship carrier Air India.

For now, Tata is heavily reliant on the profits of its cash cow, outsourcing firm Tata Consultancy Services, notes Deven Choksey, ?managing director at DRChoksey FinServ, a wealth-management firm in Mumbai. But those earnings could become more volatile if artificial intelligence supplants the sort of back-office systems that TCS provides.
"If Tata Sons is not listed, and this structure, currently, is not allowing you to raise capital, how are you going to fund such large-size investments?" said Choksey. "That's a question mark."
